back: Techniques of using live organisms or enzymes from organisms to produce products and processes useful to humans. In the restricted sense used today it refers to processes that use genetically modified organisms to achieve the same on a larger scale.

'The integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof, and molecular analogues for products and services.' Given by the European Federation of Biotechnology, and it covers both the traditional view and modern molecular biotechnology.

front: Two core techniques of modern biotechnology
back: (i) Genetic engineering — alter the chemistry of genetic material (DNA and RNA), introduce it into host organisms and change the host's phenotype. (ii) Bioprocess engineering — maintain a sterile, contamination-free ambience so that only the desired microbe or eukaryotic cell grows, in large quantities.

front: Why genetic engineering beats traditional hybridisation
back: Traditional hybridisation very often brings in undesirable genes along with the desired ones. Genetic engineering, through recombinant DNA, gene cloning and gene transfer, allows isolation and introduction of only one or a set of desirable genes without introducing undesirable genes into the target organism.

A specific DNA sequence from where replication starts; also controls the copy number of the linked DNA. Any piece of DNA linked to it can replicate within the host cells, so an alien DNA must be linked to an ori before it can multiply in the host.
Making multiple identical copies of any template DNA.

Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer linked an antibiotic resistance gene, cut from a plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium, with a plasmid vector using restriction enzymes to cut and DNA ligase to join the ends. Transferred into E. coli, it replicated using the host's DNA polymerase and made multiple copies.

front: Three basic steps in genetically modifying an organism
back: (i) Identification of DNA with desirable genes. (ii) Introduction of the identified DNA into the host. (iii) Maintenance of introduced DNA in the host and transfer of the DNA to its progeny.

An enzyme that cuts DNA at a specific position. Isolated in 1963 from E. coli, one enzyme of the pair added methyl groups to DNA and the other cut DNA; the cutting one was named restriction endonuclease.

front: Hind II and the recognition sequence
back: Hind II was the first restriction endonuclease to be isolated and characterised. It always cuts DNA at a particular point by recognising a specific sequence of six base pairs — the recognition sequence for Hind II.
First letter from the genus, next two letters from the species, then the strain, then a Roman number for the order of isolation from that strain. EcoRI = Escherichia coli strain RY 13, first enzyme.

Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of the DNA. Endonucleases make cuts at specific positions within the DNA; restriction endonucleases belong to this group, which is part of the larger class called nucleases.

A sequence of base pairs that reads the same on the two strands when the orientation of reading is kept the same — for example 5'-GAATTC-3' paired with 3'-CTTAAG-5'. It is not the same as a word palindrome such as MALAYALAM.

Single stranded overhanging stretches left on each strand because restriction enzymes cut a little away from the centre of the palindrome but between the same two bases on the opposite strands. They hydrogen-bond with complementary cut ends, which facilitates joining by DNA ligase.

front: Why the same restriction enzyme on both DNAs
back: Fragments cut by the same enzyme carry the same kind of sticky ends and can be joined end to end. Unless the vector and the source DNA are cut with the same restriction enzyme, the recombinant vector molecule cannot be created.

DNA fragments, being negatively charged, are forced to move towards the anode through an agarose matrix (a natural polymer from sea weeds). The gel sieves them by size, so the smaller the fragment, the farther it moves. Staining with ethidium bromide plus UV shows bright orange bands.
The step in which separated DNA bands are cut out of the agarose gel and the DNA is extracted from the gel piece. The purified fragments are then joined with cloning vectors.

front: Features required in a cloning vector
back: (i) Origin of replication — starts replication and controls copy number. (ii) Selectable marker — identifies and eliminates non-transformants. (iii) Cloning sites — very few, preferably single, recognition sites for the commonly used restriction enzymes. Plus vectors that work in plants and animals.

A gene that helps in identifying and eliminating non-transformants and selectively permitting the growth of transformants. Genes for resistance to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin are useful markers for E. coli, whose normal cells carry resistance to none of these.
The procedure through which a piece of DNA is introduced in a host bacterium.

Foreign DNA ligated at the BamH I site of the tetracycline resistance gene inactivates tet^R but leaves amp^R intact. Recombinants grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline; non-recombinants grow on both. rop codes for proteins involved in replication of the plasmid.

Inserting recombinant DNA within the coding sequence of an enzyme (beta-galactosidase) inactivates that gene. With a chromogenic substrate, colonies with no insert turn blue; colonies with the insert produce no colour and are identified as recombinant.

Agrobacterium tumifaciens delivers T-DNA that transforms plant cells into a tumor; its Ti plasmid has been modified into a vector that is no longer pathogenic but still delivers genes into a variety of plants. Retroviruses, which transform normal animal cells into cancerous ones, have been disarmed to deliver desirable genes into animal cells.

A host cell made able to take up DNA. Because DNA is hydrophilic and cannot cross the membrane, bacteria are treated with a divalent cation such as calcium, incubated with recombinant DNA on ice, given a brief heat shock at 42 degrees C, then returned to ice.

front: Other routes into a host cell
back: Micro-injection — DNA injected directly into the nucleus of an animal cell. Biolistics or gene gun — plant cells bombarded with high velocity gold or tungsten micro-particles coated with DNA. Disarmed pathogen vectors — infection transfers the recombinant DNA into the host.

Lysozyme for bacteria, cellulase for plant cells, chitinase for fungus, to break the cells open. RNA is then removed with ribonuclease and proteins with protease; purified DNA precipitates on adding chilled ethanol as fine threads, removed by spooling.

Polymerase Chain Reaction — multiple copies of the gene of interest are synthesised in vitro using two sets of primers (small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to regions of DNA) and DNA polymerase, which extends the primers using the nucleotides provided and the genomic DNA as template.

front: Three steps of each PCR cycle
back: (i) Denaturation — the double stranded DNA is separated by high temperature. (ii) Primer annealing — the two sets of primers anneal to the separated strands. (iii) Extension of primers — DNA polymerase extends them using the nucleotides in the reaction and the genomic DNA as template.

Isolated from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus; it remains active during the high temperature induced denaturation of double stranded DNA, so repeated cycling is possible. Repeated amplification can give approximately a billion copies of the segment.
If any protein encoding gene is expressed in a heterologous host, the protein obtained is called a recombinant protein. The gene must first be expressed under appropriate conditions after cloning.

The used medium is drained out from one side while fresh medium is added from the other, keeping cells in their physiologically most active log/exponential phase. It produces a larger biomass and so higher yields of the desired protein than a batch of small volume.

A vessel in which raw materials are biologically converted into specific products, individual enzymes, etc., using microbial, plant, animal or human cells. Large volumes of 100 to 1000 litres can be processed, with optimum temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins and oxygen.

The most commonly used type. The vessel is usually cylindrical or has a curved base to help mixing; a stirrer gives even mixing and oxygen availability. It has an agitator system, an oxygen delivery system, a foam control system, temperature and pH control systems, and sampling ports. Air may alternatively be sparged through the reactor.

The separation and purification processes that a product undergoes after the biosynthetic stage, before it is ready for marketing. The product is then formulated with suitable preservatives, put through thorough clinical trials and strict quality control testing; all of this varies from product to product.

Isolation of DNA, fragmentation by restriction endonucleases, isolation of the desired fragment, ligation into a vector, transfer into the host, culturing the host cells at large scale, and extraction of the desired product.
